title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: The Wages of Labour

What labour produces is its natural payment, or wages. In the original condition that came before anyone owned land or accumulated capital, the whole product of a person's labour belonged to that person. There was no landlord and no employer to take a share.

If that condition had continued, wages would have risen alongside every gain in productivity that the division of labour creates. Everything would gradually have grown cheaper, since each good would take less labour to make. And because goods made with equal amounts of labour would naturally trade for one another in such a world, you would also have been able to buy any given good with the product of less labour than before.

Yet even though everything would really have become cheaper, some things might have looked dearer than before, because they would trade for a larger quantity of other goods. Take an example. Suppose that in most jobs productivity rose tenfold, so that a day's work now produced ten times what it once did, but in one particular trade it rose only twofold, so that a day's work there produced merely twice what it once did. When you trade a day's output from the high-productivity jobs for a day's output from this one trade, ten times the original quantity of work in them buys only twice the original quantity in it. So a fixed amount of that one good — a pound of it, say — would seem five times dearer than before. In reality, though, it would be twice as cheap. Even though it now took five times as much of other goods to buy it, it would take only half as much labour either to buy it or to make it. Acquiring it would therefore be twice as easy as before.

But this original condition, in which the worker kept everything his labour produced, could not survive once people began to own land and accumulate capital. It was over, in other words, long before the great gains in productivity ever appeared. So there is no point tracing further what it might have meant for wages.
As soon as land becomes private property, the landlord demands a share of nearly everything the worker can grow or gather on it. His rent is the first cut taken from what farm labour produces.

The person who works the soil rarely has enough to live on until the harvest comes in. His upkeep is usually advanced to him out of the capital of an employer — the farmer who hires him — and that farmer would have no reason to hire him unless he too were to share in what the labour produced, or unless his capital came back to him with a profit. This profit is the second cut taken from what farm labour produces.

Almost all other labour is subject to the same deduction for profit. Across every craft and manufacture, most workers need an employer to advance them the raw materials, plus their wages and upkeep, until the job is done. He shares in what their labour produces — in the value it adds to the materials it is worked into — and that share is his profit.

Sometimes, of course, a single independent worker has enough capital both to buy his own materials and to support himself until the work is finished. He is at once employer and worker, and he keeps everything his labour produces, the whole value it adds to the materials. This income rolls together what are normally two separate revenues belonging to two separate people: the profits of capital and the wages of labour.

Such cases, however, are not common. Everywhere in Europe, for every independent worker there are twenty who work under an employer, and "wages" everywhere means what they usually amount to when the worker is one person and the owner of the capital that employs him is another.

What the ordinary wage works out to depends everywhere on the bargain usually struck between these two parties, whose interests are nowhere near the same. Workers want to get as much as they can; employers want to give as little as they can. Workers tend to band together to push wages up; employers band together to push them down.

It is not hard, though, to predict which side will normally win the dispute and force the other to accept its terms. Employers, being fewer, can combine far more easily. The law, moreover, either permits their combinations or at least does not ban them, while it does ban the workers'. There are no acts of Parliament against combining to lower the price of work, but plenty against combining to raise it. In any such dispute the employers can hold out far longer. A landlord, a farmer, a master manufacturer, or a merchant could generally live a year or two on the wealth they have already built up, even if they hired no one at all. Many workers could not last a week without work, few could last a month, and almost none a year. In the long run the worker may be as necessary to his employer as the employer is to him, but his need is far more immediate.

People say we rarely hear of employers combining, though we often hear of workers doing so. But anyone who concludes from this that employers seldom combine knows neither the world nor the subject. Employers are always and everywhere in a kind of tacit but constant and uniform agreement not to let wages rise above their present level. To break this agreement is everywhere a deeply unpopular act, and it brings a kind of disgrace on an employer among his neighbours and peers. We seldom hear of this combination precisely because it is the usual — one might say the natural — state of things, which nobody ever remarks on. Employers also sometimes form particular combinations to drive wages even below this level. These are always carried on with the utmost silence and secrecy until the moment they strike; and when the workers give in, as they sometimes do without a fight even though they feel it keenly, no one outside ever hears of it. Such combinations, however, are often met by a defensive combination of the workers, who sometimes also combine on their own, without any such provocation, simply to raise the price of their labour. Their stated reasons are sometimes the high price of food, sometimes the large profit their employers make from their work. But whether their combinations are offensive or defensive, we always hear plenty about them. To force a quick decision, they always resort to the loudest uproar, and sometimes to the most shocking violence and outrage. They are desperate, and they act with the recklessness of desperate men who must either starve or terrify their employers into giving in at once. The employers, on these occasions, are just as loud on their side, forever crying out for the help of the civil authorities and for the strict enforcement of the laws passed with such severity against the combination of servants, labourers, and journeymen. So the workers very rarely gain anything from the violence of these uproarious combinations, which — partly through the intervention of the authorities, partly through the greater staying power of the employers, partly through the need most of the workers are under to give in for the sake of immediate survival — generally end in nothing but the punishment or ruin of the ringleaders.

But although employers generally hold the advantage in disputes with their workers, there is nonetheless a certain level below which it seems impossible to push the ordinary wage even of the lowest kind of labour for any length of time.

A man has to live by his work, so his wages must at least be enough to keep him alive. In most cases they must be somewhat more, or he could never raise a family, and that kind of worker would die out after a single generation. On this reasoning Mr Cantillon seems to assume that the lowest sort of common labourer must everywhere earn at least double his own upkeep, so that on average he can raise two children — the wife's labour being taken as no more than enough to support herself, given that she must care for the children. But of the children born, it is reckoned, half die before reaching adulthood. So, by this account, the poorest labourers must on average try to raise at least four children, so that two have a fair chance of living that long. And the necessary upkeep of four children is supposed to come to roughly that of one grown man. The same author adds that the labour of an able-bodied slave is reckoned worth double his upkeep, and that the labour of the meanest worker, he thinks, cannot be worth less than that of an able-bodied slave. This much at least seems certain: to raise a family, the labour of husband and wife together, even in the lowest kind of common labour, must earn something more than is strictly needed for their own upkeep. But in what proportion — whether the one just mentioned, or some other — I will not undertake to decide.

There are certain circumstances, however, that sometimes give workers the upper hand and let them push their wages well above this rate, which is plainly the lowest level consistent with basic humanity.

When the demand in a country for those who live on wages — labourers, journeymen, servants of every kind — keeps rising; when each year provides work for more people than the year before, then workers have no need to combine to raise their wages. The shortage of hands sets off competition among employers, who bid against one another to get workers, and so break of their own accord through the natural agreement among employers not to raise wages. The demand for those who live on wages can clearly rise only in proportion to the rise in the funds set aside for paying wages. These funds are of two kinds: first, the revenue left over after upkeep; and second, the capital left over after what is needed to keep their employers' own businesses running.

When a landlord, an annuitant, or a man of money has a larger income than he thinks he needs to support his own family, he uses all or part of the surplus to keep one or more household servants. Increase that surplus, and he will naturally take on more such servants.

When an independent worker — a weaver or shoemaker, say — has more capital than he needs to buy his own materials and support himself until he can sell the work, he naturally uses the surplus to employ one or more journeymen so as to make a profit on their work. Increase that surplus, and he will naturally take on more journeymen.

So the demand for those who live on wages necessarily rises as a country's revenue and capital rise, and cannot possibly rise without them. The growth of revenue and capital is the growth of national wealth. The demand for those who live on wages therefore naturally rises with the growth of national wealth, and cannot possibly rise without it.

It is not the sheer size of a nation's wealth but its continual growth that drives wages up. Accordingly, the highest wages are found not in the richest countries but in the most thriving ones — those growing rich the fastest. England today is certainly a much richer country than any part of North America. Yet wages are much higher in North America than anywhere in England. In the province of New York in 1773, before the recent troubles began, common labourers earned three shillings and sixpence in local currency, equal to two shillings sterling, a day; ship-carpenters earned ten shillings and sixpence currency plus a pint of rum worth sixpence sterling, equal in all to six shillings and sixpence sterling; house-carpenters and bricklayers earned eight shillings currency, equal to four shillings and sixpence sterling; journeymen tailors earned five shillings currency, about two shillings and tenpence sterling. All these are above the London rate, and wages are said to be as high in the other colonies as in New York. Food is everywhere far cheaper in North America than in England. A famine has never been known there. Even in the worst seasons they have always had enough for themselves, though less to export. So if the money price of labour is higher there than anywhere in the mother country, its real price — the real command over the necessities and comforts of life that it gives the worker — must be higher by an even larger margin.

Though North America is not yet as rich as England, it is far more thriving, and is gaining wealth far more rapidly. The surest sign of a country's prosperity is a rise in its population. In Great Britain and most other European countries, the population is reckoned not to double in less than five hundred years. In the British colonies of North America, it has been found to double in twenty or twenty-five years. And in our own time this increase comes mainly not from the steady arrival of new settlers but from the rapid growth of the people themselves. Those who live to old age, it is said, often see fifty to a hundred descendants of their own body there, and sometimes many more. Labour is so well rewarded that a large family of children, far from being a burden, is a source of wealth and prosperity to the parents. The labour of each child, before it leaves home, is reckoned to be worth a clear hundred pounds' gain to them. A young widow with four or five small children — who among the middling or lower ranks in Europe would have little hope of a second husband — is there often courted as a kind of fortune. The value of children is the greatest of all spurs to marriage. No wonder, then, that people in North America generally marry very young. Despite the large increase such early marriages bring, there is a constant complaint of a shortage of hands in North America. It seems the demand for labourers, and the funds set aside to maintain them, grows even faster than labourers can be found to fill the jobs.

Even if a country's wealth is very great, you should not expect wages to be high there if that wealth has long stood still. The funds set aside for paying wages — the revenue and capital of its people — may be enormous; but if they have stayed at the same, or nearly the same, level for several centuries, the number of workers employed each year could easily supply, and even more than supply, the number needed the next year. There would seldom be any shortage of hands, and employers would not be forced to bid against one another to get them. Instead the workers would multiply beyond the available work. There would be a constant shortage of jobs, and the workers would have to bid against one another to get them. If in such a country wages had ever been more than enough to keep the worker alive and let him raise a family, the competition among workers and the self-interest of the employers would soon drive them down to the lowest rate consistent with basic humanity. China has long been one of the richest — that is, one of the most fertile, best cultivated, most industrious, and most populous — countries in the world. Yet it seems to have been at a standstill for a long time. Marco Polo, who visited it more than five hundred years ago, describes its farming, industry, and population in almost the same terms travellers use today. Perhaps even long before his time it had reached the full measure of wealth that its laws and institutions allow. Travellers' accounts, which disagree on much else, all agree on the low wages of labour and on how hard a worker there finds it to raise a family. If by digging the ground all day he can earn enough to buy a little rice that evening, he is content. The lot of craftsmen is, if anything, worse still. Instead of waiting idly in their workshops for customers to call, as in Europe, they roam the streets with the tools of their trade, offering their services and all but begging for work. The poverty of the lower ranks in China far exceeds that of the most wretched nations in Europe. Near Canton, it is commonly said, many hundreds — many thousands — of families have no home on land but live always in little fishing boats on the rivers and canals. The food they find there is so scanty that they eagerly scoop up the foulest garbage thrown overboard from any European ship. Any carrion — the carcass of a dead dog or cat, say — even half-rotten and stinking, is as welcome to them as the most wholesome food is to people elsewhere. Marriage is encouraged in China not by the profit of children but by the freedom to destroy them. In all the great towns, several are abandoned in the street every night, or drowned like puppies in the water. The carrying out of this horrid task is even said to be the openly acknowledged trade by which some people make their living.

China, however, though it may stand still, does not seem to be going backwards. Its towns are nowhere abandoned by their people. Land once cultivated is nowhere left neglected. So the same, or very nearly the same, amount of work must still be done each year, and the funds set aside to support it cannot have shrunk noticeably. The lowest class of labourers, then, despite their meagre subsistence, must somehow manage to keep their race going at its usual numbers.

It would be different, though, in a country where the funds set aside to support labour were noticeably shrinking. Each year the demand for servants and labourers, across all classes of work, would be less than it had been the year before. Many who had been raised to a higher class of work, unable to find a place in their own line, would gladly seek it in the lowest. That lowest class, already overcrowded with its own workers and now flooded by the overflow from all the others, would face such fierce competition for jobs that wages there would fall to the most wretched and scanty subsistence. Many would not find work even on these harsh terms, and would either starve or be driven to scrape a living by begging or by committing perhaps the worst of crimes. Want, famine, and death would at once take hold in that class and spread upward to all the higher ones, until the country's population was cut down to what the surviving revenue and capital — whatever had escaped the tyranny or disaster that destroyed the rest — could comfortably support. This is perhaps roughly the present state of Bengal and some other English settlements in the East Indies. In a fertile country that had already lost much of its population, where food should therefore not be very hard to come by, and where nonetheless three or four hundred thousand people die of hunger in a single year, we can be sure that the funds set aside to support the labouring poor are fast decaying. The difference between the spirit of the British constitution, which protects and governs North America, and that of the trading company that oppresses and lords it over the East Indies could hardly be better shown than by the contrasting condition of those two regions.

Generous pay for labour, then, is both the necessary effect and the natural symptom of growing national wealth. The bare subsistence of the labouring poor, on the other hand, is the natural sign that things have stalled, and their starving condition the sign that they are sliding fast backwards.

In Great Britain today, wages plainly seem to be more than just enough to let a worker raise a family. To convince ourselves of this, we need not go into any tedious or uncertain calculation of the lowest sum on which it could be done. There are many plain signs that wages in this country are nowhere set by that lowest rate consistent with basic humanity.

First, almost everywhere in Great Britain there is a difference, even in the lowest kind of labour, between summer and winter wages. Summer wages are always higher. But because of the extra cost of fuel, supporting a family is most expensive in winter. So since wages are highest when this expense is lowest, it is clear they are not set by what the expense requires but by the amount and presumed value of the work. It might be objected that a worker ought to save part of his summer wages to cover his winter costs, so that over the whole year his wages come to no more than is needed to keep his family through the whole year. But a slave, or anyone wholly dependent on us for his immediate survival, would not be treated this way. His daily upkeep would be matched to his daily needs.

Second, wages in Great Britain do not move with the price of food. Food prices vary everywhere from year to year, often from month to month. Yet in many places the money price of labour stays the same, sometimes for half a century at a stretch. So if in these places the labouring poor can support their families in expensive years, they must be comfortable in years of moderate plenty and well-off in years of unusual cheapness. The high food prices of the past ten years have not, in many parts of the kingdom, been matched by any noticeable rise in the money price of labour. In some parts they have — owing probably more to a rise in the demand for labour than to the rise in food prices.

Third, just as food prices vary more from year to year than wages do, so wages vary more from place to place than food prices do. The prices of bread and butcher's meat are generally the same, or nearly so, throughout most of the United Kingdom. These, and most other goods sold by retail — the way the labouring poor buy everything — are generally just as cheap, or cheaper, in large towns than in remote parts of the country, for reasons I will explain later. But wages in a large town and its surroundings are often a fourth or a fifth — twenty or twenty-five per cent — higher than a few miles away. Eighteen pence a day may be reckoned the usual rate in and around London. A few miles off it drops to fourteen or fifteen pence. Tenpence may be reckoned the rate in and around Edinburgh. A few miles off it drops to eightpence, the usual rate for common labour across most of the Lowlands of Scotland, where it varies a good deal less than in England. Such a gap in prices, which it seems is not always enough to move a man from one parish to another, would necessarily prompt the shipping of the bulkiest goods not only from parish to parish but from one end of the kingdom — almost from one end of the world — to the other, until the gap was nearly levelled out. For all that has been said about human flightiness and inconstancy, experience plainly shows that of all kinds of cargo, man is the hardest to transport. So if the labouring poor can support their families in the parts of the kingdom where wages are lowest, they must be well-off where wages are highest.
Fourth, the swings in the price of labour not only fail to match those in the price of food, in place or in time, but are often the exact opposite.

Grain, the food of the common people, is dearer in Scotland than in England, from which Scotland receives very large supplies almost every year. But English corn must sell dearer in Scotland, where it is brought, than in England, where it comes from; and, relative to its quality, it cannot sell dearer in Scotland than the Scotch corn competing with it in the same market. Grain quality depends mainly on how much flour or meal it yields at the mill, and in this respect English grain is so far superior to Scotch that, though it often looks dearer by bulk, it is generally cheaper in reality — relative to its quality, or even by weight. The price of labour, by contrast, is dearer in England than in Scotland. So if the labouring poor can support their families in one part of the United Kingdom, they must be well-off in the other. Oatmeal, it is true, supplies the common people in Scotland with the greatest and best part of their food, which is generally far inferior to that of their counterparts of the same rank in England. But this difference in diet is the effect, not the cause, of the difference in wages — though by a strange misunderstanding I have often heard it given as the cause. It is not because one man keeps a carriage while his neighbour goes on foot that the first is rich and the second poor; rather, the first is rich and so keeps a carriage, and the second is poor and so walks.

Over the course of the last century, taking one year with another, grain was dearer in both parts of the United Kingdom than during the present one. This is a fact that can no longer be reasonably doubted, and the proof is, if anything, even more decisive for Scotland than for England. In Scotland it rests on the public fiars — annual valuations, made on oath according to the actual state of the markets, of every sort of grain in every county of Scotland. If such direct proof needed any backing, I would add that the same has held in France, and probably in most of Europe. For France the proof is perfectly clear. But while it is certain that in both parts of the United Kingdom grain was somewhat dearer in the last century than now, it is equally certain that labour was much cheaper. So if the labouring poor could raise their families then, they must be much more comfortable now. In the last century the most usual day-wages for common labour across most of Scotland were sixpence in summer and fivepence in winter. Three shillings a week — very nearly the same rate — is still paid in parts of the Highlands and Western Isles. Across most of the Lowlands the most usual wage for common labour is now eightpence a day; tenpence, sometimes a shilling, around Edinburgh, in the counties bordering England — probably because of that nearness — and in a few other places where the demand for labour has lately risen considerably, around Glasgow, Carron, Ayrshire, and so on. In England, improvements in farming, manufacturing, and trade began much earlier than in Scotland. The demand for labour, and hence its price, must have risen with them. So in the last century as in the present, wages were higher in England than in Scotland. They have also risen considerably since then, though, because of the greater variety of rates paid in different places, it is harder to say by how much. In 1614 a foot soldier's pay was the same as today, eightpence a day. When the rate was first set, it would naturally have been pegged to the usual wage of common labourers, the class from which foot soldiers are usually drawn. Lord Chief Justice Hales, writing in the reign of Charles II, reckons the necessary cost of a labourer's family of six — father, mother, two children able to do something, and two who cannot — at ten shillings a week, or twenty-six pounds a year. If they cannot earn this by their labour, he supposes, they must make it up by begging or stealing. He seems to have looked into the matter very carefully. (See his scheme for the maintenance of the poor in Burn's History of the Poor Laws.) In 1688 Mr Gregory King, whose skill in political arithmetic Dr Davenant praises so highly, reckoned the ordinary income of labourers and out-servants at fifteen pounds a year per family, which he took to consist on average of three and a half persons. So his figure, though it looks different, comes very nearly to the same thing at bottom as Judge Hales's. Both put the weekly cost of such families at about twentypence a head. Both the cash income and the cash expense of such families have risen considerably since then through most of the kingdom — more in some places, less in others — though perhaps almost nowhere as much as some exaggerated accounts of present wages have lately led the public to believe. It must be noted that the price of labour can nowhere be pinned down very precisely, since different rates are often paid in the same place for the same kind of work, not only according to the worker's differing skill but according to the easiness or harshness of the employer. Where wages are not fixed by law, all we can claim to determine is what the most usual rates are; and experience seems to show that the law can never set them properly, however often it has pretended to.

The real reward of labour — the real quantity of necessities and comforts of life it can buy the worker — has, over the present century, risen by perhaps an even larger margin than its money price. Not only has grain grown somewhat cheaper, but many other things that give the industrious poor a pleasant and wholesome variety in their diet have grown a great deal cheaper. Potatoes, for example, now cost across most of the kingdom less than half what they did thirty or forty years ago. The same can be said of turnips, carrots, and cabbages — things once grown only with the spade but now commonly raised by the plough. All sorts of garden produce, too, have grown cheaper. Most of the apples, and even of the onions, eaten in Great Britain were in the last century imported from Flanders. The great improvements in the coarser branches of linen and woollen manufacture give workers cheaper and better clothing, and those in the manufacture of the coarser metals give them cheaper and better tools of trade as well as many handy and pleasant pieces of household furniture. Soap, salt, candles, leather, and fermented drinks have, it is true, grown a good deal dearer, chiefly because of the taxes laid on them. But the amount of these that the labouring poor are obliged to use is so small that the rise in their price does not offset the fall in that of so many other things. The common complaint that luxury now reaches even the lowest ranks, and that the labouring poor will no longer be content with the food, clothing, and lodging that once satisfied them, may convince us that it is not just the money price of labour that has risen, but its real reward.

Is this improvement in the condition of the lower ranks to be counted as good for society, or as a drawback? The answer seems at first perfectly plain. Servants, labourers, and workers of various kinds make up by far the largest part of every great society. And whatever improves the condition of the greater part can never count as a drawback to the whole. No society can surely be flourishing and happy when by far the greater part of its members are poor and miserable. It is only fair, besides, that those who feed, clothe, and house the whole body of the people should have a large enough share of the product of their own labour to be themselves tolerably well fed, clothed, and housed.

Poverty, though it certainly discourages marriage, does not always prevent it. It even seems to favour having children. A half-starved Highland woman often bears more than twenty children, while a pampered fine lady is often unable to bear any, and is generally worn out by two or three. Barrenness, so common among women of fashion, is very rare among those of lower station. Luxury, in women, while it may inflame the appetite for pleasure, always seems to weaken, and often to destroy altogether, the capacity to bear children.

But poverty, though it does not prevent children from being born, is extremely unfavourable to raising them. The tender plant comes up, but in such cold soil and such a harsh climate it soon withers and dies. In the Scottish Highlands, I have often been told, it is not uncommon for a mother who has borne twenty children to have only two alive. Several officers of great experience have assured me that, far from replenishing their regiment, they have never been able to keep it supplied even with drummers and fifers from all the soldiers' children born in it. Yet a finer crop of children is seldom seen anywhere than around a barracks. Very few of them, it seems, reach the age of thirteen or fourteen. In some places half the children die before they are four, in many before they are seven, and almost everywhere before they are nine or ten. This heavy mortality, however, is found everywhere mainly among the children of the common people, who cannot afford to tend them with the same care as those of better station. Though their marriages are generally more fruitful than those of the fashionable, a smaller share of their children reach maturity. In foundling hospitals, and among children raised on parish charity, the mortality is greater still than among the common people's.

Every species of animal naturally multiplies in proportion to its means of subsistence, and none can ever multiply beyond it. But in a civilized society it is only among the lower ranks that scarcity of subsistence can set limits to the further multiplication of the human race — and it can do so in no other way than by destroying a great part of the children that their fruitful marriages produce.

Generous pay for labour, by letting the poor provide better for their children and so raise more of them, naturally tends to widen those limits. It is worth noting, too, that it necessarily does this as nearly as possible in the proportion that the demand for labour requires. If demand keeps rising, the reward of labour must necessarily encourage the marriage and multiplication of workers in just such a way that a continually growing population can supply that continually growing demand. If the reward ever falls below what this requires, the shortage of hands soon raises it; and if it ever rises above it, the excessive multiplication of workers soon brings it back down to the needed rate. The market would be so understocked with labour in the one case, and so overstocked in the other, that the price would soon be forced back to the proper rate that the society's circumstances required. In this way the demand for people, like the demand for any other commodity, necessarily governs the production of people — speeding it up when it goes too slowly and slowing it down when it goes too fast. It is this demand that regulates and settles the rate of reproduction in every country of the world: making it rapidly rising in North America, slow and gradual in Europe, and altogether stationary in China.

The upkeep of a slave, it has been said, falls on his master, while that of a free servant falls on himself. Yet in reality the upkeep of the free servant is just as much at his master's expense as that of the slave. The wages paid to journeymen and servants of every kind must be enough to keep the race of journeymen and servants going, according to whether the society's demand happens to be rising, falling, or stationary. But though the upkeep of a free servant equally falls on his master, it generally costs him much less than that of a slave. The fund set aside for replacing or repairing, so to speak, a slave's wear and tear is usually managed by a careless master or a negligent overseer. The fund for the same purpose with a free man is managed by the free man himself. The disorder that generally rules the affairs of the rich naturally creeps into the management of the first; the strict thrift and careful frugality of the poor just as naturally take hold in the second. Under such different management, the same end must take very different amounts of expense to achieve. Accordingly, the experience of all ages and nations shows, I believe, that work done by free men comes cheaper in the end than work done by slaves. It is found to do so even in Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, where the wages of common labour are so very high.
Generous pay for labour, then, is both an effect of growing wealth and a cause of growing population. To complain of it is to lament the necessary cause and effect of the greatest public prosperity.

It is worth noting, perhaps, that it is in the rising state — while society is still advancing toward more wealth, rather than once it has reached its full measure of riches — that the condition of the labouring poor, the great body of the people, seems happiest and most comfortable. It is hard in the stationary state and miserable in the declining one. The rising state is in truth the cheerful and hearty state for every rank of society; the stationary state is dull; the declining one, melancholy.

Generous pay for labour, just as it encourages people to have children, also raises the industry of the common people. Wages are the spur to industry, which, like every other human quality, improves in proportion to the encouragement it gets. Plentiful food increases the worker's bodily strength, and the comforting hope of bettering his condition — of ending his days, perhaps, in ease and plenty — drives him to exert that strength to the utmost. Where wages are high, accordingly, we always find workers more active, diligent, and quick than where wages are low: in England, for instance, more than in Scotland; near great towns more than in remote country places. Some workers, it is true, when they can earn in four days enough to keep them through the week, will be idle the other three. This, however, is by no means true of most of them. On the contrary, workers paid generously by the piece are very apt to overwork themselves and ruin their health within a few years. A carpenter in London, and in some other places, is reckoned not to last at his full vigour above eight years. Something of the same happens in many other piecework trades — as most manufacturing trades are, and even country labour wherever wages are higher than usual. Almost every class of craftsmen suffers some particular ailment brought on by overdoing their particular kind of work. Ramazzini, an eminent Italian physician, has written a whole book on such diseases. We do not count our soldiers the most industrious people among us; yet when soldiers have been set to certain kinds of work and paid generously by the piece, their officers have often had to make the contractor agree that they should not be allowed to earn above a fixed daily sum at the rate they were paid. Until this was stipulated, rivalry and the desire for greater pay often drove them to overwork and harm their health by excessive labour. Excessive effort during four days of the week is often the real cause of the idleness of the other three, so loudly complained of. Great effort, of mind or body, kept up for several days running is, in most men, naturally followed by a strong craving for rest, which, unless held back by force or some pressing need, is all but irresistible. It is the call of nature, demanding relief through some indulgence — sometimes mere rest, but sometimes too dissipation and amusement. If it is not heeded, the consequences are often dangerous and sometimes fatal, and almost always, sooner or later, bring on the disease peculiar to the trade. If employers would always heed the dictates of reason and humanity, they would often have cause to moderate rather than spur on the effort of many of their workers. It will be found, I believe, in every trade, that the man who works moderately enough to be able to work steadily not only keeps his health longest but, over the course of the year, gets the greatest quantity of work done.

In cheap years, it is claimed, workers are generally lazier, and in dear years more industrious, than usual. The conclusion drawn is that plentiful food slackens their industry while scant food sharpens it. That a little more plenty than usual may make some workers idle can scarcely be doubted; but that it should have this effect on most of them — or that men in general should work better when they are underfed than when well fed, when disheartened than when in good spirits, when often sick than when generally healthy — seems most unlikely. Years of dearth, it should be noted, are generally years of sickness and death among the common people, which cannot fail to reduce the output of their industry.

In years of plenty, servants often leave their masters and trust their living to what they can earn by their own efforts. But the same cheapness of food, by enlarging the fund set aside to support servants, encourages masters — farmers especially — to hire more of them. Farmers on such occasions expect more profit from their corn by keeping a few extra labouring servants than by selling it cheap in the market. So the demand for servants rises while the number willing to fill it falls. The price of labour, therefore, often rises in cheap years.

In years of scarcity, the difficulty and uncertainty of making a living make all such people eager to go back into service. But the high price of food, by shrinking the funds set aside to support servants, inclines masters to cut rather than add to the number they keep. In dear years, too, poor independent workers often eat up the small stock with which they used to buy their materials, and are forced to become journeymen to survive. More people want work than can easily get it; many are willing to take it on worse terms than usual; and the wages of both servants and journeymen often sink in dear years.

Masters of all kinds, then, often strike better bargains with their servants in dear years than in cheap ones, and find them more humble and dependent in the former than in the latter. Naturally, therefore, they praise dear years as more favourable to industry. Landlords and farmers, besides — two of the largest classes of masters — have another reason to be pleased with dear years: the rents of the one and the profits of the other depend heavily on the price of food. Nothing, however, could be more absurd than to imagine that men in general work less when they work for themselves than when they work for others. A poor independent worker will generally be more industrious than even a journeyman paid by the piece. The one keeps the whole product of his own effort, the other shares it with his master. The one, in his separate independent state, is less exposed to the temptations of bad company, which in large workshops so often ruin the morals of the other. The independent worker's superiority over servants hired by the month or the year — whose wages and upkeep are the same whether they do much or little — is likely to be greater still. Cheap years tend to raise the proportion of independent workers to journeymen and servants of all kinds, and dear years to lower it.

A French writer of great knowledge and ingenuity, Mr Messance, receiver of the taille in the election district of Saint-Étienne, tries to show that the poor do more work in cheap years than in dear ones, by comparing the quantity and value of goods produced in those different conditions in three different industries: one of coarse woollens, carried on at Elbeuf, and one of linen and another of silk, both spread across the whole generality of Rouen. From his account, copied from the registers of the public offices, it appears that the quantity and value of goods made in all three industries has generally been greater in cheap years than in dear ones, and has always been greatest in the cheapest years and least in the dearest. All three seem to be stationary industries — ones whose output may vary somewhat from year to year but which, on the whole, are neither advancing nor declining.

The linen manufacture of Scotland and the coarse woollen manufacture of the West Riding of Yorkshire are growing industries, whose output, though with some variation, is generally rising in both quantity and value. But on examining the published accounts of their annual output, I have not been able to find that its variations bear any noticeable relation to the dearness or cheapness of the seasons. In 1740, a year of great scarcity, both industries did indeed decline considerably. But in 1756, another year of great scarcity, the Scotch industry advanced more than usual. The Yorkshire industry did decline, and its output did not climb back to its 1755 level until 1766, after the repeal of the American Stamp Act. In that year and the next it far exceeded anything it had reached before, and it has gone on advancing ever since.

The output of all great industries that sell at a distance must depend not so much on the dearness or cheapness of the seasons in the countries where they operate as on the conditions affecting demand in the countries where they are consumed — on peace or war, on the prosperity or decline of rival industries, and on the good or bad mood of their chief customers. Besides, much of the extra work probably done in cheap years never enters the public industry registers. The menservants who leave their masters become independent labourers. The women return to their parents and commonly spin, to make clothes for themselves and their families. Even the independent workers do not always produce for public sale, but are employed by some of their neighbours to make goods for household use. So the product of their labour often makes no figure in those public registers — the records of which are sometimes published with such fanfare, and from which our merchants and manufacturers would vainly pretend to proclaim the prosperity or decline of the greatest empires.

Although the swings in the price of labour not only do not always match those in the price of food, but are often the exact opposite, we must not on that account suppose that the price of food has no effect on the price of labour. The money price of labour is necessarily governed by two things: the demand for labour, and the price of the necessities and comforts of life. The demand for labour — according to whether it is rising, stationary, or falling, or whether it calls for a rising, stationary, or falling population — settles the quantities of necessities and comforts that must be given to the worker; and the money price of labour is settled by what it takes to buy that quantity. So although the money price of labour is sometimes high where food is cheap, it would be higher still — demand remaining the same — if food were dear.

It is because the demand for labour rises in years of sudden and unusual plenty, and falls in years of sudden and unusual scarcity, that the money price of labour sometimes rises in the one and sinks in the other.

In a year of sudden and unusual plenty, many employers of industry hold funds enough to support and employ more workers than they had the year before; and this extra number cannot always be found. So those employers who want more workers bid against one another to get them, which sometimes raises both the real and the money price of their labour.

The opposite happens in a year of sudden and unusual scarcity. The funds for employing industry are smaller than the year before. A good many people are thrown out of work and bid against one another to get it, which sometimes lowers both the real and the money price of labour. In 1740, a year of unusual scarcity, many people were willing to work for bare subsistence. In the years of plenty that followed, it grew harder to find labourers and servants. The scarcity of a dear year, by reducing the demand for labour, tends to lower its price, while the high price of food tends to raise it. The plenty of a cheap year, on the contrary, by raising demand, tends to raise the price of labour, while the cheapness of food tends to lower it. In the ordinary swings of food prices, these two opposite forces seem to cancel each other out — which is probably part of the reason why wages are everywhere so much steadier and more lasting than food prices.

A rise in wages necessarily raises the price of many goods, by raising the part of their cost that resolves into wages, and so far tends to reduce their consumption both at home and abroad. But the very thing that raises wages — the growth of capital — also tends to raise productivity, so that a smaller quantity of labour produces a greater quantity of work. The owner of the capital that employs a large number of workers necessarily tries, for his own advantage, to divide and arrange their work so well that they produce the greatest possible quantity. For the same reason he tries to supply them with the best machinery that he or they can devise. What happens among the workers in a single workshop happens, for the same reason, among the workers of a whole society. The greater their number, the more naturally they divide themselves into different classes and subdivisions of work. More minds are set to inventing the best machinery for carrying out each task, and so it is more likely to be invented. There are many goods, therefore, which through these improvements come to be produced with so much less labour than before that the rise in the price of labour is more than offset by the fall in the amount of it required.
